title: Street Intersection Finder: Where Streets Cross
description: Locate where two streets cross in a town with the Street Intersection Finder — junction coordinates from the open map. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, 'meet at 5th and Main' becomes coordinates you can drop into any map — assuming your town's 5th and Main actually cross, which the finder also settles.
quick_answer: The Street Intersection Finder locates where two named streets cross within a town, using OpenStreetMap, and gives you the junction's coordinates. Enter the town, type the two street names, and read the crossing — the meeting point, the landmark, the address-less address every city conversation runs on.

faq: How does it find the crossing?
It matches both street names within the town's OpenStreetMap record and computes where their lines cross, returning the junction's coordinates.
What if the streets never cross?
You get an honest 'no crossing' — parallel streets and near-misses resolved by data rather than by hope. Check name spellings, then accept the geography.
Can I use the tool without sharing my precise location?
Yes — the town is typed; your location plays no part.
Why might a boundary or place name look different elsewhere?
Street names change (renamings, honorary names) and other sources hold different vintages; the record here is OpenStreetMap's.
Does MapBench store my browser location?
No.
Streets crossing twice?
Curved and looping streets can intersect at two points; both are reported with the map to choose between.
Highways and ramps?
Junctions of major roads resolve where the record models them; interchange geometry can make 'the crossing' a small region rather than a point.
A street with two names?
Dual-named streets match by either recorded name in most cases — try the alternate if the first fails.
Coordinates format?
Latitude/longitude for the junction — paste them into any tool on this site, from Distance Calculator onward.
Intersection of a street with itself?
Looping streets do cross themselves occasionally — the finder reports genuine self-junctions where the record models them, geography's little joke.
City not listed?
The finder searches within the town scope you give; a very small settlement may need its county or nearest town as the scope, then the street names do the rest.
